garden.identify: Tiny pear-shaped insects, green, black or pink, with two little tailpipes at the rear. Sticky honeydew and ants tending them are the giveaway.
garden.note: Rarely worth spraying. A hard jet of water knocks them off, and lady beetles and hoverflies arrive within a week or two if you leave them alone.

garden.name: Tomato hornworm
garden.where: Tomatoes, peppers and potatoes — find them by the dark pellets of frass on leaves below.
garden.identify: A very large green caterpillar with white chevrons and a stiff horn at the rear. It hides in plain sight.
garden.note: Hand-pick — but if it wears white cocoons, leave it: parasitic wasps have already won. The adult is the big sphinx moth that hovers at dusk.

garden.name: Cabbage white
garden.where: Any brassica: kale, cabbage, broccoli, mustards.
garden.identify: A plain white butterfly with one or two black wing spots. The caterpillar is velvety green and lies along a leaf vein.
garden.note: The single most reliable pest of a brassica bed. Floating row cover from the day you transplant is the whole answer.

garden.name: Colorado potato beetle
garden.where: Potatoes, and eggplant when the potatoes run out.
garden.identify: A round beetle with ten black stripes on a cream back; orange egg clusters and fat pink humpbacked larvae underneath the leaves.
garden.note: Squash the orange eggs on the leaf underside twice a week and you will rarely need to do anything else. Famously resistant to insecticides.

garden.name: Squash bug
garden.where: Squash and pumpkins, hiding under leaves and at the base of stems.
garden.identify: A flat grey-brown shield-shaped bug; bronze egg clusters laid in neat V patterns in the angle of leaf veins.
garden.note: Lay a board beside the plants overnight — they gather under it and you can collect them at dawn. Rub the bronze eggs off with your thumb.

garden.name: Squash vine borer
garden.where: Inside the stem at the base of a squash plant.
garden.identify: The adult is a day-flying orange-and-black moth that looks like a wasp. The damage is sudden wilting plus sawdust-like frass at the stem base.
garden.note: The reason a healthy zucchini collapses overnight in July. Bury a couple of leaf nodes so the vine roots at several points, and plant a second succession in early July.

garden.name: Japanese beetle
garden.where: Roses, grapes, beans and raspberry leaves, feeding in groups in full sun.
garden.identify: Metallic green body with copper wing covers and small white tufts along the sides. Leaves are skeletonised to lace.
garden.note: Knock them into soapy water first thing in the morning while they are sluggish. Traps pull in more beetles than they catch — put them at the far end of the property or not at all.

garden.name: Slugs
garden.where: Under mulch, boards and pots; out at night and after rain.
garden.identify: The silvery slime trail and ragged holes in the middle of leaves, not at the edges.
garden.note: Worst in a wet spring on the coast. Beer traps, a night patrol with a flashlight, and iron-phosphate bait all work; salt does not belong in soil.

garden.name: Cucumber beetle
garden.where: Cucumbers, melons and squash, from the moment the seedlings emerge.
garden.identify: Small and yellow with three black stripes down the back, or with twelve spots.
garden.note: The real harm is bacterial wilt, which it carries — a beetle-free plant rarely wilts. Row cover until flowering, then remove it so bees can work.

garden.name: Flea beetle
garden.where: Eggplant, arugula, radish and young brassicas.
garden.identify: Tiny shiny black beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed, leaving leaves peppered with shot-holes.
garden.note: Cosmetic on a big plant, fatal on a seedling. Cover new transplants for the first three weeks and they will outgrow it.

garden.name: Spider mites
garden.where: Hot, dry, dusty conditions — greenhouse tomatoes, beans, and anything against a sunny wall.
garden.identify: Leaves take on a fine bronze stippling; fine webbing appears in the leaf axils. Tap a leaf over white paper to see the moving specks.
garden.note: Dry air is what lets them explode. Hosing the undersides of leaves regularly is the simplest control.

garden.name: Cutworms
garden.where: Just under the soil surface beside a transplant; feeding at night.
garden.identify: Fat grey-brown caterpillars that curl into a tight C when you dig them up. A seedling severed cleanly at ground level is the sign.
garden.note: A cardboard collar pushed 2 cm into the soil around each transplant ends the problem for the season.

garden.name: Earwig
garden.where: Dark damp crevices by day; feeding on soft growth and ripe fruit at night.
garden.identify: Slim brown insect with a pair of pincers at the rear.
garden.note: Genuinely both — it chews seedlings and dahlia petals, and it also eats aphids and codling moth eggs. A rolled newspaper or a stuffed flowerpot traps them if numbers get out of hand.
